subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: All the interdependent, enzyme-controlled chemical reactions in an organism
The breakdown of food molecules in mitochondria to release the energy that cells need for all their activities
Only the reactions that build macromolecules such as proteins and glycogen from their monomers
The reactions that happen outside cells during digestion
items.note: Metabolism = anabolism + catabolism, interlinked. Trap: picking only catabolism (respiration) or only anabolism.

items.stem: Which process is an example of anabolism?
choices: Hydrolysis of starch in the small intestine
Oxidation of pyruvate in respiration
Formation of glycogen from glucose
Digestion of proteins into amino acids
items.note: Anabolism builds macromolecules by condensation (glycogen, protein synthesis, photosynthesis). The other three break molecules down (catabolism).

items.stem: Why does an enzyme catalyse only one or a few reactions?
choices: It is made of only one type of amino acid, so it can only attract one type of molecule
Its active site's shape and chemistry are complementary to specific substrates
It is used up after it catalyses a reaction, so it cannot meet a second substrate
It works at only one exact temperature, and other reactions need a different one
items.note: Specificity comes from the 3D shape and chemistry of the active site. Enzymes are not used up, and they work over a range of temperatures.

items.stem: In the induced-fit model of enzyme action:
choices: The active site is rigid and its shape already matches the substrate exactly, like a key in a lock
The substrate changes shape but the enzyme does not
The enzyme changes shape only after the products have been released from the active site
Both the substrate and the active site change shape when binding occurs
items.note: The guide expects you to say both change shape on binding; this strains bonds in the substrate. The rigid version is the older lock-and-key model.

items.stem: The active site of an enzyme is formed by only a few amino acids. Why can a change to an amino acid far from the active site still stop catalysis?
choices: Interactions between amino acids across the whole molecule hold the active site in its precise 3D shape
Amino acids far from the active site bind the substrate first and pass it on to the active site
Every amino acid in the enzyme takes part directly in breaking the bonds of the substrate
Distant amino acids supply the activation energy that the substrate needs to react
items.note: The tertiary structure as a whole maintains the active site. Changing a distant residue can alter folding and so the active-site shape.

items.stem: Increasing temperature from 10 °C to 30 °C increases the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction mainly because:
choices: The active site expands as the protein warms, so more substrate molecules fit into it at once
The enzyme starts to denature, which unfolds the protein and exposes extra active sites
Molecules move faster, so substrate–active site collisions happen more often and with more energy
The activation energy of the reaction increases, so the products that form store more energy
items.note: Collision theory: more kinetic energy → more frequent and more successful collisions. Denaturation only becomes important above the optimum.

items.stem: Above its optimum temperature the rate of an enzyme reaction falls steeply. The best explanation is:
choices: The substrate molecules move too fast to stay in the active site long enough to react
The enzyme is used up faster at high temperature because each molecule reacts more often
Water evaporates from the mixture, so the enzyme and substrate become too concentrated
Bonds holding the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape and substrate no longer binds
items.note: Denaturation is a structural change in the enzyme; substrate cannot bind to the altered active site. It is usually permanent.

items.stem: At high substrate concentration the rate of an enzyme reaction reaches a plateau. This is because:
choices: The high concentration of substrate begins to denature the enzyme by changing the pH
Nearly all active sites are occupied at any moment, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting
The products build up and always inhibit the enzyme competitively, cancelling any extra substrate
The activation energy of the reaction rises as more substrate molecules are added to the mixture
items.note: At saturation, adding substrate cannot increase the number of enzyme–substrate complexes formed per second. Add more enzyme to raise the plateau.

items.stem: Statins lower cholesterol production by binding to the active site of an enzyme in the cholesterol pathway. Statins are therefore:
choices: Non-competitive inhibitors, which bind to an allosteric site and lower the maximum rate permanently
Competitive inhibitors, whose effect can be reduced by raising substrate concentration
Mechanism-based inhibitors, which bind permanently to the active site and destroy the enzyme
Allosteric activators, which change the active site so it binds cholesterol instead
items.note: Binding at the active site and competing with the substrate = competitive. High substrate concentration out-competes the inhibitor, so the maximum rate can still be reached.

items.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. Compared with the uninhibited reaction, the rate at very high substrate concentration will be:
choices: Lower, because the inhibitor changes the active site shape and adding substrate cannot reverse this
The same, because a large excess of substrate out-competes the inhibitor for the active site
Higher, because the inhibitor binds allosterically and holds the active site open for substrate
Zero, because a non-competitive inhibitor permanently destroys every enzyme molecule present
items.note: Non-competitive inhibitors bind to an allosteric site; the maximum rate (plateau) is lowered and extra substrate does not restore it. That is the graph difference from competitive inhibition.

items.stem: In the pathway threonine → (enzyme 1) → … → isoleucine, a high isoleucine concentration slows the whole pathway. This happens because isoleucine:
choices: Competes with threonine for the active site of the last enzyme in the pathway, blocking it
Denatures every enzyme in the pathway, so they must be resynthesised before it restarts
Binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme, so less product is made when it is not needed
Is converted back into threonine by the same enzymes, so the substrate keeps being recycled
items.note: End-product (feedback) inhibition acts on the first enzyme of the pathway, through an allosteric site. It is reversible, so the pathway restarts when isoleucine is used up.

items.stem: Penicillin binds irreversibly to the active site of the bacterial enzyme transpeptidase. This is an example of:
choices: End-product inhibition
Competitive, reversible inhibition
Denaturation by heat
Mechanism-based inhibition
items.note: Penicillin forms a permanent covalent bond with the active site, so the enzyme can no longer build cross-links in the cell wall. Irreversible = mechanism-based.

items.stem: Which pair are correctly matched as a cyclical and a linear metabolic pathway?
choices: Krebs cycle (cyclical); glycolysis (linear)
Glycolysis (cyclical) and Calvin cycle (linear)
Krebs cycle (linear) and Calvin cycle (cyclical)
Glycolysis (cyclical) and Krebs cycle (linear)
items.note: The Krebs and Calvin cycles regenerate their starting compound; glycolysis is a chain from glucose to pyruvate.

items.stem: Explain why enzymes in the human body produce heat as a by-product, and how this is useful to mammals.
markscheme: Metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient in energy transfer (1)
Some energy is lost as heat in each reaction (1)
Mammals (endotherms) use this heat to keep body temperature constant/high (1)
Higher body temperature keeps enzyme rates high (1)
items.tactic: State the inefficiency first, then link it to a consequence for the organism.

items.stem: Describe how the effect of pH on the activity of an enzyme can be explained.
markscheme: Each enzyme has an optimum pH where the rate is highest (1)
A change in pH alters the charges on amino acids (R groups) of the active site (1)
Ionic/hydrogen bonds in the tertiary structure are disrupted (1)
The active site changes shape so the substrate binds less well (1)
items.tactic: Describe the shape of the curve first, then explain each side using charges and bonds.

items.stem: Compare and contrast competitive and non-competitive inhibition.
markscheme: Both reduce the rate of reaction (1)
Competitive inhibitor binds the active site; non-competitive binds an allosteric site (1)
Competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate in shape; non-competitive does not need to (1)
Competitive: effect overcome by raising substrate concentration; non-competitive: it is not (1)
Competitive: same maximum rate eventually; non-competitive: lower maximum rate (1)
items.tactic: Compare-and-contrast needs at least one similarity plus paired differences in the same sentence.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student measured the volume of oxygen released from hydrogen peroxide by catalase extracted from an invented plant at five temperatures. Oxygen released in 2 minutes (cm³): 10 °C 4.0; 20 °C 7.8; 30 °C 12.4; 40 °C 15.1; 50 °C 3.2.
(a) Calculate the mean rate of oxygen release at 30 °C, in cm³ per minute. (b) Describe and explain the trend from 10 °C to 50 °C. (c) Suggest one improvement to find the optimum temperature more precisely.
markscheme: (b) Rate rises from 10 °C to 40 °C (4.0 to 15.1 cm³) (1)
More kinetic energy so more frequent successful substrate–active site collisions (1)
Rate falls sharply above 40 °C (to 3.2 cm³ at 50 °C) because the enzyme denatures / active site changes shape (1)
(c) Test more temperatures between 40 °C and 50 °C (e.g. every 2 °C) with repeats (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
